report:
Your view is **broadly supported, but not ironclad**. The key positive evidence is a multicenter randomized trial in *NEJM* concluding chlorhexidine–alcohol gave a significantly lower surgical-site infection risk after cesarean than iodine–alcohol: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048. A Cochrane review is more cautious: chlorhexidine gluconate is “probably slightly” better than povidone-iodine for preventing SSI after caesarean, with moderate-certainty evidence: https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section. A focused systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI compared with povidone-iodine solutions: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/.

The main caveat is that not every later trial replicated a clear win: the open-label CAPICA trial concluded povidone-iodine should still be considered acceptable for cesarean antisepsis: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/. Overall, the evidence favors chlorhexidine–alcohol, especially alcohol-based preparations, but effects may be modest and context-dependent; iodine-based antisepsis remains an acceptable alternative when chlorhexidine is unsuitable.
